clues.text: A falling orchard fruit supposedly triggered an entire mechanical revolution in physics.
Invented calculus while sheltering at home during an infectious bubonic plague quarantine.
Used glass prisms to prove that white sunlight is composed of rainbows.
Every schoolchild memorises three fundamental movement laws to survive tenth-grade science exams.
Born in Woolsthorpe Manor, Lincolnshire, later studying at Trinity College, Cambridge.
Honoured by having the standard international unit of physical force named after him.
Built the first practical reflecting telescope using curved mirrors instead of lenses.
Often hailed alongside Albert Einstein as the towering father of classical physics.
The only individual in history awarded Nobel Prizes across two different sciences.
Discovered the chemical elements polonium and radium after boiling tons of pitchblende.
Her century-old personal laboratory notebooks remain dangerously radioactive and stored in lead.
Drove portable radiological X-ray vehicles nicknamed Little Curies along World War battlefields.
Her pioneer radiation work laid the foundation for modern hospital cancer radiotherapy.
Born in Warsaw, Poland, before moving to Paris for university education.
Won her initial physics accolade in nineteen-oh-three alongside her husband Pierre.
Carried glowing radioactive glass test tubes inside her laboratory apron pockets casually.
Albert Einstein later redefined it as curved spacetime rather than invisible force.
Galileo allegedly dropped unequal spheres off the Leaning Tower of Pisa.
The reason your phone screen reliably shatters when slipping out of pockets.
Astronauts grow slightly taller aboard the International Space Station without its compression.
Dictates oceanic tidal bulges on Earth through cosmic pulls from the Moon.
First quantified mathematically in the sixteen-eighty-seven masterpiece Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica.
Celebrated with constant value nine-point-eight meters per second squared in physics problem sets.
Known to high-school students as the weakest of the four fundamental forces.
Nicknamed Lightning Bolt while flashing his iconic signature diagonal archer pose.
Proved human sprinters can casually glance sideways and celebrate before finishing races.
Ate dozens of fried chicken nuggets daily while sweeping gold medals in Beijing.
Set the electric world sprint record of nine-point-five-eight seconds in Berlin.
Hails from Sherwood Content in Trelawny, representing the sprint powerhouse Jamaica.
Untied running shoelaces did not stop him from breaking world records effortlessly.
Won eight Olympic gold medals across three consecutive summer Olympic Games appearances.
The universal reference whenever someone runs surprisingly fast to catch a bus.
Formalised as a standalone mathematical number and concept by ancient astronomer Brahmagupta.
Earliest recorded physical dot numeral found on the ancient Indian Bakhshali manuscript.
Dividing any number by this innocent digit instantly causes calculator computer crashes.
Revolutionised global mathematics after Arab scholars transmitted the numeral system into Europe.
Ancient Roman numerals had no symbol for it, making complex arithmetic impossible.
Looks like an empty circle, symbolizing absolute nothingness yet granting power.
India's greatest intellectual gift celebrated in every patriotic school quiz contest.
Appeared in formal algebraic treatise Brahmasphutasiddhanta in the year six-twenty-eight.
Stands elegantly along the southern banks of the Yamuna River in Agra.
Commissioned by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan to enshrine his empress Mumtaz Mahal.
Its four corner minarets were deliberately tilted outward to protect the dome.
Constructed from translucent white Makrana marble that changes color with morning sunlight.
The mandatory tourist photo pose where visitors pretend to pinch its dome.
Designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in nineteen-eighty-three as a masterpiece.
Voted onto the New Seven Wonders of the World list in 2007.
Universally described in poetry as a solitary teardrop on the cheek of time.
Marched two-hundred-and-forty miles to the seashore to make tax-free salt by boiling water.
Revered as the Father of the Nation and addressed affectionately as Bapu.
Spun raw cotton thread daily on a portable wooden hand-operated charkha wheel.
Born in the coastal town of Porbandar, Gujarat, in eighteen-sixty-nine.
His bespectacled smiling portrait graces every official Reserve Bank of India banknote.
Nominated five times for the Nobel Peace Prize but never actually awarded.
Pioneered mass civil disobedience using the philosophy of non-violence, or Satyagraha.
Returned permanently from South Africa to India in nineteen-fifteen to lead freedom.
Vanaras constructed a floating stone bridge across ocean straits to reach Lanka.
Composed originally in classical Sanskrit verse by the ancient sage-poet Valmiki.
A divine golden deer acts as an illusion to lure princes away.
The return of its righteous hero inspires the nationwide autumn festival Diwali.
The central narrative begins in the historic solar dynasty capital of Ayodhya.
During its Sunday eighties television broadcast, Indian city streets emptied out completely.
Regarded as the Adikavya, the very first poetic epic of Indian literature.
Spread across Southeast Asia, inspiring national royal ballet traditions in Thailand and Indonesia.
Towering peak officially measured at eight-thousand-eight-hundred-and-forty-eight-point-eight-six meters above sea level.
Straddles the international Himalayan border between Nepal and the Tibet Autonomous Region.
First officially summitted in nineteen-fifty-three by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay.
The summit still contains fossilised marine limestone from an ancient seabed floor.
Locally venerated as Sagarmatha in Nepal and Chomolungma in Tibetan tradition.
The default metaphor for any impossibly difficult college assignment or project task.
Climbers must navigate the dangerous crevasse-ridden Khumbu Icefall using tied aluminum ladders.
Named in nineteenth-century surveys after the former British Surveyor General of India.
Tested thousands of materials before carbonised bamboo filament burned for hours reliably.
Commercially perfected by Thomas Edison at his Menlo Park industrial research laboratory.
The universal cartoon symbol drawn hovering above someone's head having brilliant ideas.
Early versions lost over ninety percent of their consumed energy as heat.
A sealed glass orb housing a delicate coiled tungsten metal wire filament.
Patented as an electric lamp for commercial manufacture in eighteen-eighty.
First illuminated New York City financial district streets through a central pearl station.
The groundbreaking invention that officially freed human society from darkness and candle-wax.
Formulated the world's most famous equation relating physical mass directly to energy.
Visualised himself riding alongside a beam of light during teenage thought experiments.
Famously refused to wear socks because his big toes always made holes.
Won the nineteen-twenty-one Nobel Prize for explaining the photoelectric effect, not relativity.
Used as the universal sarcastic nickname whenever someone states the obvious.
A famous black-and-white photograph shows him sticking his tongue out at photographers.
Born in Ulm, Germany, later serving as an examiner in Bern's patent office.
The wild-haired archetype of the eccentric genius across modern pop culture.
First intelligible spoken sentence summoned an assistant after accidentally spilling battery acid.
Alexander Graham Bell was granted the groundbreaking patent after beating rival Elisha Gray.
The historic acoustic telegraph patent was officially awarded in eighteen-seventy-six.
Has evolved into handheld glass rectangles that consume seven hours of daily screentime.
The inventor refused to keep one in his study fearing constant interruptions.
Vintage rotary dials required sticking fingers into numbered holes and spinning clockwise.
First successful two-way long-distance conversation transmitted between Boston and Cambridge, Massachusetts.
The device that permanently eliminated the agonizing wait for postal paper letters.
Jan Ingenhousz proved green leaves require sunlight exposure to generate breathable oxygen.
The classic five-mark chemical diagram every Indian student drew with green pencils.
Joseph Priestley kept mice alive under glass jars using small mint sprigs.
Microscopic green chloroplasts containing chlorophyll molecules capture photons inside leafy cells.
Over half of Earth's oxygen comes from oceanic microscopic phytoplankton, not trees.
Melvin Calvin won a chemistry Nobel Prize for tracing its carbon cycle.
Operates inside plant mesophyll layers, sucking atmospheric carbon dioxide through open stomata.
Nature's solar-powered kitchen that feeds almost every living creature on Earth.
Solved the impossible Gordian knot legend by simply drawing his sword and slicing.
Born in Pella, ancient kingdom of Macedonia, as the son of King Philip.
Tamed an unrideable fiery warhorse simply by turning it toward the sun.
Undefeated military commander tutored in philosophy by Aristotle during his teenage years.
Carried the long eighteen-foot Macedonian pike called the sarissa across vast continents.
Founded over twenty global cities, naming almost every single one after himself.
Referred to in Indian history textbooks as Sikandar whose army refused crossing the Beas.
Conquered the mighty Achaemenid Persian Empire before dying young in three-twenty-three BC.
Stands tall on a rocky desert plateau just outside Cairo, Egypt.
Remained the tallest human-made structure in the world for over three thousand years.
Internet conspiracy theorists still aggressively insist extraterrestrial visitors helped build their corners.
Aligned with incredible geographic precision toward true astronomical north without modern compasses.
The only surviving ancient wonder from the original list of the Seven.
Constructed from over two million massive carved limestone and granite blocks.
The classic textbook illustration that introduced schoolkids to Pharaohs and mummies.
Erected as grand royal tombs around two-thousand-five-hundred BC during Old Kingdom rule.
Legend says he dropped cannonballs off the Leaning Tower to time descents.
Spotted four major celestial moons orbiting Jupiter, dismantling Earth-centered universe models.
Spent his final decade under house arrest after angering the Roman Inquisition.
Handcrafted a spyglass tube using curved glass lenses to study the moon.
Born in Pisa, Tuscany, later teaching geometry and astronomy in Padua.
Published starry astronomical observations in Sidereus Nuncius in sixteen-hundred-and-ten.
Crowned by modern historians as the undisputed father of observational astronomy.
Queen famously screamed his name five times in Bohemian Rhapsody's operatic section.
Surprisingly invented first for shaping ceramic clay pottery before being used for transport.
Archaeological evidence traces its earliest forms back to Mesopotamia around thirty-five-hundred BC.
Described in the popular phrase warning people against reinventing proven fundamental ideas.
Thriving Pre-Columbian Mesoamerican civilizations built stone cities without ever using it for carts.
A circular wooden disc fitted with axles and eventually radial wooden spokes.
Early builders rolled massive heavy temple stones over felled logs before making it.
Oldest wooden axle specimen was excavated in the marshes near Ljubljana, Slovenia.
Heralded in history textbooks as humanity's most revolutionary mechanical invention ever.
Traditionally dictated by sage Vyasa and inscribed by elephant-headed deity Ganesha.
One of the longest epic poems in world literature, spanning over one-hundred-thousand shlokas.
A fateful game of dice between cousins stripped an entire royal family of kingdom.
Contains the divine philosophical dialogue delivered between charioteer and warrior on Kurukshetra.
The central dynastic seat of power was the Kuru capital city of Hastinapura.
B.R. Chopra's televised Sunday adaptation famously brought regular Indian life to a standstill.
Features a climactic war lasting exactly eighteen days involving millions of warriors.
Revered across Indian tradition as the Panchama Veda, or the fifth Veda.
Five interlocking coloured rings on a white background representing unity of five continents.
The ceremonial torch flame is lit using sunlight and mirrors at ancient Olympia.
The first modern international edition was hosted in Athens in eighteen-ninety-six.
Originated in ancient Greece as athletic festivals honoring Zeus, accompanied by sacred truces.
Live pigeon shooting and tug-of-war were once official medal sporting events.
Athletes stand on multi-tiered podiums receiving gold, silver, or bronze medals while anthems play.
The reason people suddenly become armchair experts on archery and shooting every four years.
The world's greatest multi-sport spectacle running on a strict four-year cycle.
Rises proudly on the Champ de Mars along the Seine River in Paris.
Built as a temporary entrance arch for the eighteen-eighty-nine World's Fair.
Grows up to fifteen centimeters taller during summer heatwaves due to thermal expansion.
Constructed from over eighteen-thousand puddle iron parts held together by thermal rivets.
Designed by the civil engineer who also built the Statue of Liberty's skeleton.
The undisputed default desktop wallpaper and poster choice for college aesthetic rooms.
Affectionately called the Iron Lady by French citizens across the world.
Parisians initially despised the lattice tower, writing petitions demanding its immediate demolition.
